justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with modest upward drift over longer horizons. For the 1-day estimate of 680, I was anchoring heavily on recent price action and momentum, assuming that whatever level was prevailing at the time of the forecast would persist with only minor fluctuation driven by intraday noise. The 1-week estimate of 683 adds a small positive drift, reflecting a slight bullish bias based on the broader trend context, while the 1-month estimate of 690 extends that drift further, implying a gradual grind higher consistent with underlying fundamental or macro support but without expecting any sharp directional move.

The confidence interval widths expand predictably with time horizon, which reflects the compounding of uncertainty over longer periods. For the 1-day window, the interval is relatively tight at plus or minus roughly 25 points because short-term price behavior tends to be more mean-reverting and less subject to structural shifts. By one week, the interval widens to reflect the possibility of a meaningful catalyst — an economic data release, a central bank communication, or a geopolitical development — that could shift sentiment more decisively. By one month, the interval spans 180 points, acknowledging that over that timeframe, entire narrative regimes can shift, earnings seasons can reset expectations, or macroeconomic conditions can deteriorate or improve substantially.

The key risks that could push outcomes outside these stated intervals fall into two broad categories: sharp upside surprises and sharp downside shocks. On the upside, an unexpected positive catalyst such as a major policy pivot, a blowout earnings report, or a resolution of a geopolitical flashpoint could drive prices well above 780 on the one-month horizon. On the downside, a financial stability event, a sudden deterioration in credit conditions, or an inflation surprise that forces aggressive monetary tightening could push prices well below 600, invalidating the lower bound of my one-month interval.

It is also worth acknowledging that my intervals implicitly assume a relatively normal distribution of outcomes without fat tails, which is a simplification. Real financial markets exhibit skewness and kurtosis that can make extreme moves more likely than my stated confidence intervals suggest. If volatility were to spike — say, due to a liquidity event or a correlated sell-off across asset classes — the actual distribution of outcomes would be considerably wider than what I have represented here, particularly at the one-month horizon.
